title: Music — Piano and Guitar, three-year programme (2026)
description: Piano and Guitar across NGG's three years — Year 1 Foundation, Year 2 Developing, Year 3 Advanced — 24 weekly 90-minute lessons a year in two terms, broadened from the NGG Piano and Guitar term plans. Members move through the years by mastery (finish 80% of a year and the next opens), with support and stretch work in every lesson and an Essentials strand (theory, reading, ear, instrument care, practice habits, performance, Nigerian music history, technology, business, leadership). Covers technique, scales and keys, chords and inversions, reading and rhythm, ear training, improvisation, West African and contemporary styles (rock, ballad, hip-hop, reggae, Afrobeats, highlife, gospel), accompanying, ensemble and composition, with revision, tests and a showcase each term. Every lesson has objectives, a practice routine, a weekly assignment, a theory check and a marked practice task.
source: NGG Piano and Guitar curriculum (programme team), broadened to a standard three-year progression: Year 1 about Grade 1–2, Year 2 about Grade 3–4, Year 3 about Grade 5 and leadership

lessons.title: Introduction to the piano
lessons.summary: The keyboard, how to sit and how to hold your hands — the habits every pianist builds on.
objectives: You will find middle C and every C on the keyboard
You will sit at the right height and distance with curved fingers
You will number your fingers 1 to 5 on each hand
lessons.body:
## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Shoulders loose: roll them back three times
- Tap each finger on your knee, 1 to 5, both hands

## Learn (30 minutes)

The keyboard repeats a pattern of **two black keys and three black keys**. C is the white key just left of the two black keys; **middle C** is the C nearest the centre. Sit so your forearms are level with the keys, back straight, feet flat. Curve your fingers as if holding a small ball. Thumb is finger 1, little finger is 5, on both hands.

## Play (40 minutes)

- Find and play every C, low to high, with finger 3
- Play C D E F G with right hand fingers 1–5, then back down
- Play C B A G F with left hand fingers 1–5

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Find every C, D and E on the keyboard with your eyes closed, then check
1. Five-finger pattern on C, hands separately, slowly
1. Name the white keys out loud as you play them

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Instrument care:** keep the lid closed when you finish, never put drinks on the piano, and wipe the keys with a dry cloth.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Learn the names of all seven white keys (C D E F G A B) and play the C five-finger pattern hands separately every day.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Building scales on C
lessons.summary: How a major scale is built from tones and semitones, and playing C major with the correct fingering.
objectives: You will explain the major scale pattern T-T-S-T-T-T-S
You will play C major one octave, hands separately, with a thumb-under
You will build the scale on D, G and F with the same pattern
lessons.body:
## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Five-finger pattern on C, both hands
- Clap four steady beats, then eight

## Learn (30 minutes)

A **semitone** is the very next key (black or white); a **tone** is two semitones. Every major scale follows **Tone–Tone–Semitone–Tone–Tone–Tone–Semitone**. Right hand fingering for C major: 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5 (the thumb passes under after E). Left hand: 5 4 3 2 1 3 2 1.

## Play (40 minutes)

- C major, right hand, slowly; say the finger numbers
- C major, left hand, slowly
- Work out D major with the pattern: it needs F♯ and C♯

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. C major one octave, each hand, 5 times a day
1. Write out the notes of G and F major using the pattern
1. Play G major (one sharp: F♯) and F major (one flat: B♭) slowly
1. **With a tool —** Find the song on YouTube and use the playback-speed control (or a free slow-downer app) to take it to 0.5× without changing the pitch. Learn it slowly and correctly, then step the speed back up.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Practice habits:** practise little and often — 20 focused minutes every day beats two hours on Friday. Keep a practice log: date, what, how long, what improved.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Construct and play the major scales on D, G and F — write the notes down first, then play each one octave, hands separately.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Chords on C — and your first song
lessons.summary: Major triads built from the scale, and accompanying a gospel song with them.
objectives: You will build a major triad from notes 1, 3 and 5 of a scale
You will play C, F and G major chords in the left hand
You will accompany "Lord You Are So Good" with block chords
lessons.body:
## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- C major scale, both hands separately
- Play C–E–G one note at a time, then together

## Learn (30 minutes)

A **triad** is three notes stacked in thirds: the 1st, 3rd and 5th notes of the scale. C major = C–E–G; F major = F–A–C; G major = G–B–D. These three are chords **I, IV and V** in C — the chords most songs are built from.

## Play (40 minutes)

- Block chords C, F, G in the left hand, four beats each
- Play the melody of "Lord You Are So Good" in the right hand
- Put them together: chord on beat 1, melody on top

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Build triads on D, G and F: write them, then play them
1. Change C → F → G → C without stopping, 10 times
1. Play the song with block chords at a slow, steady tempo
1. **With an AI assistant —** ask it, or a chord-finder site, for the chords of a song you love. Then CHECK it at the instrument — chord sites are often wrong by a bar or a whole key. Finding the mistake is the exercise.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Theory:** the musical alphabet is only A to G, then it repeats. A sharp (♯) raises a note by a semitone, a flat (♭) lowers it.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Construct the chords on D, G and F (D–F♯–A, G–B–D, F–A–C) and play each as a block and broken chord.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Legato and staccato — and a rock groove
lessons.summary: Two touches every pianist needs, on the five-finger patterns of C, D, G and A minor, at 100 bpm.
objectives: You will play legato (smooth, joined) and staccato (short, detached)
You will play pentascales on C, D, G and A minor at 100 bpm
You will play a steady rock rhythm with the left hand
lessons.body:
## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Pentascale on C, legato, hands together
- Metronome on at 80, then 100

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Legato** means each note joins the next — lift one finger only as the next goes down. **Staccato** means short and bouncy — the note is released quickly, from the wrist. A **pentascale** is the first five notes of a scale. A minor uses the white keys from A: A–B–C–D–E.

## Play (40 minutes)

- Pentascales C, D, G, Am legato at 100 bpm
- The same pentascales staccato
- Rock: left hand plays root eighth-notes (C C C C) while the right hand plays the chord on beats 2 and 4

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Each pentascale legato, then staccato, at 100 bpm
1. Rock groove on C–F–G–C for two minutes without stopping
1. Listen to two rock songs and tap along to the beat
1. **With a tool —** Search for a backing track in this key ("C major backing track 70bpm") and play along. Playing to someone else's time is a different skill from playing alone, and it is the one a band needs.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Listening:** listen to one song this week and name the instruments you hear. Drums, bass, keys, guitar, voice — where does each sit?

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Bring and play five songs in the rock style — at least one on the piano with the rock left-hand pattern.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Blocked and broken chords — the ballad
lessons.summary: Playing C major blocked and D major broken at 100 bpm, and the gentle broken-chord pattern ballads are built on.
objectives: You will play a chord blocked (all at once) and broken (one note at a time)
You will keep a broken-chord pattern steady at 100 bpm
You will accompany a ballad with a 1–5–8 left-hand pattern
lessons.body:
## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- C major and D major triads, blocked
- Same triads broken, up and down

## Learn (30 minutes)

A **blocked** chord plays all its notes together. A **broken** chord plays them one after another (an *arpeggio*). Ballads use slow broken chords in the left hand — root, fifth, octave (1–5–8) — so the melody can sing on top.

## Play (40 minutes)

- Blocked C major, broken D major, 100 bpm
- Ballad pattern 1–5–8 on C, Am, F, G
- Add a simple right-hand melody over the pattern

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Blocked and broken C and D at 100 bpm, 3 minutes
1. Ballad progression C–Am–F–G, slowly and evenly
1. Choose a ballad you love and find its chords

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Reading:** the treble clef (𝄞) curls round G; the lines are E G B D F (Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit), the spaces F A C E.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Bring and play five songs in the ballad style — at least one with the 1–5–8 broken-chord left hand.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Both hands, the I–IV–V–I progression — and hip-hop
lessons.summary: Placing both hands on pentascales together and playing the I–IV–V–I progression that underpins hip-hop and pop.
objectives: You will play pentascales with both hands together
You will play I–IV–V–I in C, F and G
You will play a hip-hop pattern with a syncopated left hand
lessons.body:
## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Pentascale C, hands together
- Chord I–IV–V–I in C, blocked

## Learn (30 minutes)

Hands together is a new skill: start slowly so both hands land at exactly the same time. **I–IV–V–I** in C is C–F–G–C; in G it is G–C–D–G; in F it is F–B♭–C–F. Hip-hop keys often loop four bars with the left hand playing **off the beat** (syncopation).

## Play (40 minutes)

- Pentascales hands together on C and G
- I–IV–V–I in C, G and F
- Hip-hop loop: right hand chords on 1 and the 'and' of 2; left hand bass on 1 and 3

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Hands together pentascales, 5 minutes
1. I–IV–V–I in three keys, slowly
1. Loop the hip-hop pattern for one minute without stopping

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Body:** warm up your hands and wrists before playing, and stop if anything hurts. Pain is a signal, not a challenge.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Playing from a fakebook: "Holy Are You Lord"
lessons.summary: Reading a lead sheet — melody with chord symbols — and turning it into a full piano part.
objectives: You will read chord symbols above a melody
You will play the melody in the right hand and chords in the left
You will perform "Holy Are You Lord" from start to finish
lessons.body:
## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- I–IV–V–I in C
- Pentascale on G, hands together

## Learn (30 minutes)

A **fakebook** (lead sheet) shows only the melody and the chord symbols, like C, G/B, Am, F. You 'fake' the accompaniment: the left hand plays the chord named above each bar while the right hand plays the tune. A slash chord such as **G/B** means a G chord with B in the bass.

## Play (40 minutes)

- Read the lead sheet: name every chord
- Left hand chords only, in time
- Right hand melody only
- Together, slowly, then at performance tempo

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Hands separately, then together, 15 minutes
1. Play it for someone at home
1. Mark the bars that still break and practise just those

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Performance:** an audience remembers the feeling, not the mistakes. Practise starting and finishing confidently.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Perfect "Holy Are You Lord" — play it through with no stops, and record it.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Two-octave C major and A minor — reggae
lessons.summary: Extending scales over two octaves, the relative minor, and the reggae 'skank' on the off-beat.
objectives: You will play C major and A natural minor over two octaves
You will explain why A minor is the relative minor of C
You will play a reggae off-beat chord pattern
lessons.body:
## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- C major one octave, both hands
- A minor pentascale

## Learn (30 minutes)

**A minor** uses the same notes as C major, starting on A — it is C's **relative minor**. Two-octave scales need a second thumb-under (right hand) or finger-over (left hand). Reggae places short chords on the **off-beat** (beats 2 and 4, or every 'and') while the bass plays a laid-back line.

## Play (40 minutes)

- C major two octaves, hands separately
- A minor two octaves, hands separately
- Reggae: right hand short chords on the 'and' of every beat, left hand roots on 1

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Two-octave C and Am, hands separately, 5 times each
1. Reggae pattern on Am–G–F–G, 2 minutes
1. Listen to a reggae song and clap the off-beat
1. **With a tool —** Search for a backing track in this key ("C major backing track 70bpm") and play along. Playing to someone else's time is a different skill from playing alone, and it is the one a band needs.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Reading:** the bass clef (𝄢) dots surround F; its lines are G B D F A (Good Boys Do Fine Always), the spaces A C E G.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Play C major and A minor two octaves hands separately, and play one reggae song with the off-beat chord pattern.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Revision
lessons.summary: Bringing weeks 1–8 together: scales, chords, touches and styles, ready for the test.
objectives: You will play every scale and chord from this term from memory

lessons.body:
## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- All pentascales C, D, G, Am
- I–IV–V–I in C, G, F

## Learn (30 minutes)

Revision is **targeted practice**: test yourself, find the weak spot, fix it. Go through this list and tick what you can do at 100 bpm without stopping: C/D/G/F major one octave; C and Am two octaves; triads on C, D, G, F; legato and staccato; blocked and broken chords; I–IV–V–I in three keys; one song in each style (rock, ballad, hip-hop, reggae); "Holy Are You Lord".

## Play (40 minutes)

- Self-test the checklist with a partner
- Spend most of the time on the two weakest items
- Run through "Holy Are You Lord"

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Each day, play the checklist once and mark it
1. Spend 10 minutes on the weakest item
1. Play your best song for someone

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Practice habits:** before revising, write down what you *can't* yet do. That list is your practice plan.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

lessons.title: Rhythm and reading: note values and time signatures
lessons.summary: Reading rhythm properly — note values, rests and 4/4 and 3/4 time — so new music can be learned from the page.
objectives: You will read whole, half, quarter and eighth notes and their rests
You will count and play in 4/4 and 3/4
You will sight-read a short melody in C
lessons.body:
## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Clap and count four bars of quarter notes, then eighth notes

## Learn (30 minutes)

A **time signature** tells you how many beats are in a bar (top number) and which note gets the beat (bottom number). In **4/4** count 1-2-3-4; in **3/4** (waltz) count 1-2-3. Whole = 4 beats, half = 2, quarter = 1, eighth = ½. Rests have the same values in silence.

## Play (40 minutes)

- Clap rhythm cards in 4/4 and 3/4
- Sight-read a 4-bar melody in C, right hand
- Play a waltz-style left hand: root on 1, chord on 2 and 3

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Clap and count one rhythm line each day
1. Sight-read one new short piece (MuseScore has free beginner pieces)
1. Practise the waltz pattern on C–G–C
1. **With an AI assistant —** ask it for four short sight-reading exercises at your level. Check each one BEFORE you play it: are the notes inside the key, do the bars add up to the time signature? Models get notation wrong, and finding the bad bar is the real exercise. Play each sound one ONCE. Sight-reading only improves on music you have not seen before.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Theory:** dotted notes add half their value — a dotted half note lasts 3 beats; a tie joins two notes into one longer sound.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.summary: Preparing and performing a short programme for the class — performance is a skill too.

lessons.body:
## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Run your two pieces once, slowly

## Learn (30 minutes)

A performance has three parts: **introduce** (name, piece, style), **perform** (keep going even if you slip — the audience rarely notices), **bow** and thank the audience. Choose one piece from this term and one in a different style.

## Play (40 minutes)

## Learn (30 minutes)

objectives: You will play melody and bass together

lessons.body:
## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Finger-style places the **melody on the top strings** and the bass with the thumb. Start from the chord shape, find the melody note within or near it, and keep the thumb steady.

## Play (40 minutes)

- Thumb bass alone
- Melody alone
- Combine slowly

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Thumb bass alone
1. Then: Combine slowly
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Performance:** practise your stage routine — tune, check, count in, play, finish together — until it is automatic.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Add harmonics to your arrangement.

## This week's assignment

Arrange a short melody finger-style and record it.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Juju and highlife bands use **two or more guitars interlocking**: one plays a repeating high riff, another plays thirds or sixths, the bass guitar locks with the talking drum. Afrobeats keeps this — short, bright, repeating lines.

## Play (40 minutes)

- Learn riff B
- Interlock with a partner

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Theory:** modes are scales starting on each note of the major scale. Dorian (from the 2nd) and Mixolydian (from the 5th) are common in pop, funk and gospel.

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.

**Nigerian music history:** fuji and apala grew from Yoruba Islamic music; Afrobeat's horns and long grooves came from Fela and Tony Allen. Listen to one track of each.

- Graduation recital
- Portfolio

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Graduation recital
1. Then: Portfolio
1. Record one take and listen back
